# Walter Burkert — Das Lied von Ares und Aphrodite (1960)

## Bibliographic identity

The original is Walter Burkert, "Das Lied von Ares und Aphrodite: Zum Verhältnis von Odyssee und Ilias," *Rheinisches Museum für Philologie* 103 (1960): 130–144. The journal-level metadata (author, title, volume, year, page span) is verified; a PDF of the German original has been located on the journal's own site (rhm.uni-koeln.de) but its sentences have not yet been extracted into this house. An English translation exists as "The Song of Ares and Aphrodite: On the Relationship between the Odyssey and the Iliad," in G. M. Wright and P. V. Jones, eds., *Homer: German Scholarship in Translation* (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1997), reported at pages 249–262; that page span is unverified and the translation volume has not been added as a container of its own. Until extraction, the German article is the citable object and the English span is provisional.

## Source scholarship

Burkert's 1960 article is a classic of Homeric philology on precisely the passage the essay reads. Its demonstrandum is intertextual: through repeated lines, formulas, and phrases shared between the Demodocus song and the divine comedy of *Iliad* 1, Burkert argues that the song presupposes the *Iliad* — the Odyssey-poet is not drawing on a common stock but composing against a known text, and the gods' comic detachment in Odyssey 8 is intelligible as a deliberate transformation of the Iliadic divine apparatus. The article thereby became a standard reference in the analyst/unitarian and neoanalysis debates about the relation of the two epics, and any use of the song's poetics that ignores it is scholarly incomplete.

What makes the article close to load-bearing for the essay is the reading reported at its interpretive center: the song as a celebration of *technē* over *physis*. On this account — reported via the Bryn Mawr Classical Review notice (BMCR 1998.11.09) of the Wright and Jones translation volume — the craft-god's victory over the war-god is the Odyssey-poet's programmatic answer to Iliadic force: the poem that begins from cunning and homecoming stages, inside its own performance scene, the defeat of the strongest god by the cleverest. A 1960 philological classic thus already reads the episode as a verdict about craft-intelligence versus violent strength, which is exactly the hinge on which the essay turns the scene toward its own technological reading. The essay does not need Burkert to go further than this — and he does not: his frame is poetics and intertextuality, not technology.

The evidentiary situation must be kept honest. No sentence of Burkert's — German or English — has yet been extracted and verified by this house. The technē-over-physis characterisation currently rests on a reviewer's summary of a translation of the article. That is a legitimate pointer for locating the argument but not a quotable authority; the German PDF is in hand as a locator, and extraction of the exact sentences (with page numbers in RhM 103) is the single task standing between this house and citation-grade use.

## Essay use

### Source's relevant contribution

Burkert supplies the philological control: a canonical scholarly demonstration that the Demodocus song is a deliberate, intertextually knowing composition whose point is the victory of craft over force — securing the essay against the objection that its craft-versus-strength reading is a modern imposition on a light entertainment.

### Licensed essay use

- Cite the article as the standard demonstration that the song presupposes *Iliad* 1 and transforms its divine comedy.
- Once sentences are extracted: attribute the technē-over-physis reading of the song to Burkert, with exact wording and page.
- Serve the myth history as the philological anchor of the episode's scholarly reception.

### Claim boundary

Burkert's claim concerns Odyssey/Iliad intertextuality and the song's poetics — craft over force as a poetic program. He does not read the net as proto-technology-critique, does not treat surveillance, apparatus, or enframing, and says nothing about modernity. The passage from his technē/physis verdict to the essay's enframing reading is the essay's own Argued move. Until the German text is extracted, even the technē-over-physis attribution must be flagged in draft prose as reported via BMCR.
